utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On Thursday, the 13th of November, 2008, I bid good morning to the accused, the Prosecution, counsel, and the witness, of course, whom I will not forget, and the registrar, the usher, and the court reporter. Let me first read an oral decision before we continue with the testimony of this witness, because next week we're going to have Mr. Tomic, and the Chamber is going to render this decision which is rather long, so I'll go slowly. Oral decision regarding the question of the Prosecution to be given an additional 1 hour, 35 minutes for the examination of Witness Tomic. At the hearing of the 12th of November, 2008, the Prosecution requested 1 hour and 35 additional minutes for the examination of Witness Tomic, who will be appearing from the 17th to the 19th of November. In support of its request, the Prosecution said it needed to raise precise issues with witness Neven Tomic, and the time would be longer than the time left to them, that is, 2 hours and 17 minutes. The question has to do with the federation between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was envisaged at a certain point in time. In more general terms, the Prosecution also refers to a disequilibrium between the total amount of time given to the Defence to examine and cross-examine witnesses on the one hand, and the time allotted to the Prosecution for the cross-examination of a witness. The counsels of Stojic, Praljak, Petkovic, and Coric objected to the request of the Prosecution. In a preliminary manner, the Chamber recalls that in line with guiding line number 5, the Prosecution has for the cross-examination a hundred per cent of the time allotted for the examination-in-chief. As for the time available for the cross-examination conducted by Defence counsel, the Chamber has ruled that they should have a total - that is all the Defence teams conducting cross-examinations - 50 per cent of the time allotted for the examination-in-chief. The Chamber presents in detail the motives behind such a decision based on the guiding line for the presentation of evidence dated on the 24th of April, 2008, and refers the Prosecution to those grounds developed in that decision. This guiding line was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber by the decision of the 18th of July, 2008, a decision prompted by an appeal by the Defence of Petkovic and Praljak and not by the Prosecution. The Chamber does not find that there is any imbalance in the implementation of this guiding line. The witness Neven Tomic appeared before the Chamber from the 27th to the 30th of October, 2008, and on the 3rd and 4th of November, 2008. According to the calculation of time as communicated by the registrar, the Prlic Defence used 8 hours, 6 minutes for the examination-in-chief of this witness. The Defence counsel 2D, 3D, and 4D used a total of 3 hours and 17 minutes for the cross-examination. Finally, the Prosecution used 5 hours and 49 minutes for the cross-examination of this witness, so that the Prosecution has available 2 hours and 17 minutes to complete their cross-examination. However, at the hearing of the 4th of November, 2008, the Chamber, on an exceptional basis, allotted 2 hours to the Prlic Defence to proceed with additional examination of the witness. The Prlic Defence, therefore, had globally used a total of 10 hours and 6 minutes. The Chamber notes that under these circumstances, in order to establish a fair balance, it is appropriate to grant the Prosecution the additional 1 hour and 35 minutes requested. The Chamber therefore grants the request of the Prosecution. So the Prosecution will have a total of 3 hours and 52 minutes to continue and complete their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just for clarification for the record. I want to make sure we're abundantly clear on this. I indicated that I would need about two hours for redirect examination. Therefore, your findings, I believe, are incorrect that I was granted two hours. I indicated I would need about two hours. Now, in light of you giving the Prosecution an hour and a half, I will probably need one additional hour. So I'm asking at this point three, perhaps as much as four hours for redirect examination. The problem is every time you cave in to the Prosecution's whims and fancies, this is what happens. They're asking for additional time without having made a proper basis. It should be at the conclusion, it should be at the conclusion of their cross-examination that they should make that -- that request that they need additional time. If you go back, if you go back and you look at their cross-examination, they waste 60 per cent of it initially going over material that's already in the record. They then come at the end of their time and like Oliver Twist with cup and can; then they say we want more time. This is a ridiculous way of allocating time in advance prior to them at least putting on the cross-examination. In the future, what I will be doing is I will be objecting on the grounds that the material has been covered on direct examination and, therefore, they're wasting their time. Your Honour, I want to make sure we understand ourselves very clearly. I do not object when they cover ground already established on direct examination because the way I see it is they're wasting their time, and now what you're doing is you're giving them more time. You're encouraging them. That's what's happening, and your findings are absolutely incorrect. And therefore, I'm putting down my marker at this point in time that I'm going to need at least an additional one hour based on additional time that you gave them, which I think is unfounded based on the reasonings that they gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, the one thing we mustn't do, of course, is make a submission immediately after ruling by Your Honours, which amounts in substance to an appeal. Your Honour, we would just like to say on the record, and this we know already from brief discussion, is the position of Ms. Nozica and Mr. Khan's client that the decision Your Honours have just delivered with great respect is deeply flawed in the way that you have equated the various times. But Your Honour, I'm not going to argue it as if it were an appeal, but it is absolutely deeply flawed. What we do do is we strongly support Mr. Karnavas in everything he said in relation to further time for re-examination because it must follow, Your Honours, that when the Prosecution has more time for cross-examination, if -- and if they don't, then why are they having more time, if they do cover more ground of substance - because we certainly hope they will; otherwise, the whole thing will have been a wasteful exercise - if they cover more ground of substance, then necessarily in fairness the Defence counsel who is re-examining must be given appropriately more time to cover the ground. Otherwise, justice just didn't done because in the end, it isn't a question of timing. After all, Your Honours' decision is recognising these matters as guidelines. Your Honours must give, with respect, Mr. Karnavas the fair time he needs to cover the ground, to be reviewed, of course, ultimately after the cross-examination when we see whether this extra time has in fact led to covering ground of any further substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'll be ever so brief. But I do think given the comments that have been made, there has to be some, again, balance injected into the record. First of all, I'm grateful to the Chamber for the time, and I want to be very clear that the first thing I say is thank you for the additional time to all the Judges. Having said that, I suppose in many respects I'm not particularly happy with the analysis of the Chamber, either. The Prosecution -- so I guess we're all unhappy this morning. I'm happy with the final result. I'm not so happy with the Chamber's analysis. I do think that there is an unfairness being practiced on the Prosecution in general. The Prosecution will continue to state its concerns, as we feel that we are duly obligated to do so, but I'm most grateful for the additional time of this particular witness. Your Honour, Mr. Karnavas's comments are really, well, unfortunate. I'll leave it at that. I don't think we used our time improperly. I think we covered helpful material, and I think ultimately the Chamber hopefully found helpful and will continue to find helpful is that with conducted -- is any examination conducted with 100 per cent efficiency? Probably not. It's the nature of the beast. There's a matter of art, not science, but you -- to say that it was covered in direct is -- doesn't say anything. Of course things were covered in direct; hence, the scope of direct; hence, cross-examination. So -- but that doesn't mean the Prosecution nor the Chamber has to accept what the -- whether the case put by the Defence in their direct or the answers given by the witness. We don't have to accept that at face value. Of course we can go back and challenge that, so that just doesn't go anywhere. Now, if -- you know, to turn back on the Defence what has just been said to the Prosecution, if at the end of the cross -- all the total cross-examination, Mr. Karnavas with articulate a reason for additional time for redirect, of course he can -- he can attempt to do so, but I -- I must observe that say -- to say baldly and as a general matter that if the Prosecution has -- is given an hour and 35 minutes of additional time, which is still substantially less time than the Defence took, substantially less, that for -- in return for an hour and 35 minutes, he gets an hour, almost equal amount of addition many time in redirect, is frankly preposterous. Again, I'll end where I started by saying I thank you to the Chamber, to each of you Judges for the additional time, and we will proceed, and I hope you will find the time well used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me give you an example, a concrete example. Yesterday, we were talking about constituent peoples. It seems every time we have a new Prosecutor in here, we go through the same ground. It happen with Ms. West. It happened a while back with Mr. Stringer. They don't have the singlest clue about what a constituent nation is. For three years, we've been talking about this. Now, if you go back and you look at the transcript with Judge May, who is a very experienced Judge from England who sat here, and you look at that transcript, he would cut off counsel and say, Counsel, that's already been established, move on. Counsel, that's already been established, move on. Continually, throughout the process, he kept reins. Now, I've been keeping my powder dry because if the Prosecution wishes to waste their time on cross, that's their time. I'm not going to interfere. But now I'm put in a position where I continually will have to object on the grounds that they're going over established facts, wasting their time, in order to wear down the witness to then ask for more time, showing you statistics, and with statistics somehow claiming that numbers should be equated, and that's not how trials are conducted. I find it very odd that this is the approach that has been taken, and just as the Prosecution said yesterday, well, I think I need an hour and a half more without giving a basis, that's the foundation that I give for saying I need one more hour because they're going to -- going to additional information; and with that, I think at this point I'm going to make an oral submission for interlocutory appeal on this issue because I think we are opening up a Pandora's box. Part of my redirect examination has to directly contradict matters that were brought up by the other Defence. That's why I think the Trial Chamber is moving rather hastily in granting this request by the Prosecution who simply shows numbers, brings out the violin, and all of a sudden we're supposed to feel sorry that they're being hampered. My client has been waiting for years to get a fair trial. This is not turning out to be a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we raise the question, what's Mr. Scott so worried about? Presumably by getting more time for cross-examination, he's expecting and hoping to strengthen his case and get more material out of the witness. In those circumstances, why is he so dismissive of, then, Mr. Karnavas having more time for re-examination? Because the more Mr. Scott does achieve out of cross-examination, the more clear it is that, in fairness, the Defence should have time for re-examination. And what is Mr. Scott so scared about? If he's going to get what he wants out of -- out of cross-examination and if it is going to be solid evidence, then why isn't he more relaxed about allowing re-examination because then -- well, Mr. Scott, I'll sit down, and then I will allow you to stand up when I sit down which I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll wait --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But I'll sit down, Mr. Scott, because I don't really much care for the practice, with respect, Your Honours, of two counsels standing up in court at the same time. So I'm going to sit down and give the floor to Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Your Honour, I didn't intend to respond further, but those comments are extremely personal and I think, again, highly unfortunate. I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will stand up to counsel and make an exception. Of course they're not personal, Your Honour. Mr. Scott happens to be the lead Prosecutor making the submissions for the Prosecutor. I do claim I rarely, if ever, and I'd like to claim never, I do not make personal comments about counsel in this court. I challenge anybody to find on the record that I've adopted that practice. No. Mr. Scott is the representative of the Prosecution, and everything I say is a submission about the Prosecution. But of course I name him as a courtesy because he is the counsel submitting on behalf of the Prosecution at this moment. Mr. Scott, through Your Honours, no, of course it's not personal. Please accept that assurance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I might have the floor, Your Honour. If I might have the floor for a moment since the Defence have once again gone on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would like to have the floor when everyone else is finished. I'm being patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Prlic, then. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do not wish to make any comments regarding the ruling. It has not surprised me. You can give the Prosecutor all the time in the world, and that will not assist him. Already in the initial stages of the proceedings, I gave up my rights to an effective trial to give time to the Prosecutor to prove something that I do not think can be proven in any way. So I'm not talking about the merits, but I wish to speak about the grounds and argumentation for this decision. My request is that this piece of paper given by the Prosecutor should be given an IC number. Why? It is my opinion that it is a paradigm of the overall proceedings here, and unfortunately, also of the manner of decision-making. Look at the arguments. The same applies to your ruling. You say the Defence, and that is flagrantly incorrect. There are Defences here. There are six Defences here. We accept adding up apples and pears. I don't know who wrote this paper, maybe Ms. Tabeau. These things are incomparable. A comparison is made by the time used by the Defence in the cross-examination with the time used by the Prosecution in this part of the Defence case. First of all, my Defence did not have a single 92 bis or 92 ter witness, so only viva voce time is not comparable. Furthermore, as an example of lengthy examination by the Defence, the Witness RA has been cited, and this is a witness who admitted his -- confessed his guilt, and a part of the document was his admission and the facts established on that occasion. Therefore, these are things that cannot be compared. I'm talking about the arguments given in this case. What I wish to say is that my Defence counsel, and I believe the others, too, wish to be treated individually. I asked for the separation of the indictment twice. The Chamber rejected this both times. I did not write the indictment. I did not confirm it, but I request to have the same rights as the other accused. I do not wish to have a sixth of the rights enjoyed by the late Milosevic, Momcilo Perisic, or Seselj. No one agrees with that, not even the people I have mentioned, and that is why this is not my problem. It's a problem for this Tribunal. And let me say once again, you can give all the time you wish to the Prosecutor. He uses it mostly to undermine the credibility of all the witnesses that are being brought here. That is common to all of them, from the first to the last, for the presidents of states, for the prime ministers, for ministers, ambassadors. Perhaps Bosnia and Herzegovina is not such a well-known state, but for me it is important, and I represented it. It is perhaps not like Switzerland, the United States, France, or Hungary. Those countries are in quite a different situation. The Prosecutor may address a request for compromising material for a particular witness from a country in the region, and they have to find something. If they don't, then the Prosecutor can say that that country is not cooperating. [In English] I have the right to say that. This is very important issue. [Interpretation] The Prosecution can say that country is not cooperative, and then the ability of that country going to the European Union is questioned. So to summarise, I would like an IC number to be given to this piece of paper because I think it is a paradigm of all the arguments that are being presented in this case. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Good morning, Your Honours. I apologise to Mr. Scott, though I was on my feet before him, but he said he would speak at the end. I just wish to make one point. I know the ruling is such as it is once it has been made, but something is not clear to me once again. We had an earlier decision regarding instructions how time would be calculated, and it was said that the time given to the Prosecution for the cross would correspond to -- a hundred per cent to the time for the examination-in-chief, but with today's ruling we have a slightly different situation. That is calculating the time used by the Defence in the direct examination, and we are told in advance the amount of time that will be used in the redirect. I'm referring to a hypothetical situation when the Defence will not know until the Prosecution completes their cross-examination how much time that Defence will need for redirect, particularly as we have already seen during the cross-examination of the Prosecution that certain issues are being raised with the permission of the trial that were not covered in the direct because they are relevant. For example, myself. When presenting Mr. Coric's Defence, I will not know whether I will need a redirect and how long it will last. So if my redirect is lengthy because of something said by the Prosecution, then Mr. Scott or somebody else may get on its feet and say the Defence is having so much time and I had so much and then I wish some -- to have some additional time. So this is leading to a vicious circle. I appeal to the Chamber to reconsider its decision and see where this could lead us in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm happy to wait until after Mr. Scott has addressed the Court. I just want to note that after he speaks, I would ask for five minutes to make some observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. If this is going to go on and on, with all due respect, I'd like to hear all the Defence comments, and I'll respond all at one time. I've been sitting here waiting. I think I'm owed that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Khan, conclude and then Mr. Scott will conclude, and we'll stop there because we are here for a witness, and for the sake of this witness it's necessary that he thinks we have him in mind, and at the moment we're evidently not thinking about the witness. So Mr. Khan, do proceed so that Mr. Scott can then conclude, and then we will bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm much obliged. The last comment of my learned friend is perhaps indicative of some of the problems in this courtroom. It is: "I think I'm owed that much." This case, this trial, and this institution is not about the rights of individuals. It's about, obviously, the fair administration of justice, and one does see a tendency, and I would respectfully submit an extremely unfortunate tendency, in this courtroom to reduce matters completely unnecessarily down to the personal sensibilities of the actors in the courtroom. This is not about -- this case is not about Mr. Khan or Mr. Karnavas or Mr. Scott. It's about facts that Your Honours are deciding, and counsel that are as experienced as the advocates in this courtroom and certainly as able and capable as my learned friends for the Prosecution really should -- all of us, all of us should have somewhat thicker skin than perhaps we have shown in this case thus far. One can trenchantly and robustly criticise one's opponents without it being viewed as a personal assault or an ad hominem attack. Of course, arguments should be politely constructed, but vivid language can be used, and personal offence should not be taken, because what it does, it wastes time, it distracts, and it adds heat to the courtroom and lends no light whatsoever. Your Honour, yesterday I made a submission and Your Honours have, of course, ruled, but it's well known the saying that there are lies, darned lies, and statistics; and one cannot reduce a fair trial to a simple mathematical formula. Your Honours, I won't say more about that, but on behalf of Mr. Stojic, we do join my learned friend Mr. Karnavas in supporting an oral application for interlocutory leave to appeal given the reasoning, not the ultimate decision only, but the reasoning of the Trial Chamber in coming to this decision. I would concur, with respect, to my learned friend Mr. Stewart. For the life of me, I cannot see why there is any prejudice to the Prosecution. Well, firstly, I don't know why the Prosecution are apparently a little bit -- are so concerned about matters, but in the event that additional time has been given, Your Honours have made a ruling that the Defence -- each Defence team has a certain amount of time. If Mr. Karnavas and later on if we decide in re-examination that in the interests of justice additional time is needed - and we're not asking for additional time globally; we're simply saying we'll take time from another witness and use it in re-examination - why that would prejudice the Prosecution, why that would be somehow inappropriate. I simply do not see it, Your Honours. Your Honours, a margin of discretion always must be given to the Prosecution as they know their case, and a margin of discretion must be given to the Defence. We are not simple labourers hauled off the streets without knowledge. There are some very experienced advocates here, and I think the way a courtroom will work is sometimes to give trust to the parties when they say they do need additional time because they know their case better than anybody else. And so, Your Honours, I would ask that a significant margin of appreciation be given when Mr. Karnavas asks for additional time or later on if we ask for additional time. My final point, and again, it's an awful American saying, but I will say it. You know, what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander, but -- well, I'm not keen on it, but, Your Honours, Mr. Scott, my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you translate this in an understandable language because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- I understand the words, but there must be some meaning behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it's parity of treatment. It's parity of treatment, to put it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: -- more succinctly and in, perhaps, English. But, Your Honours, yesterday I mentioned that the application as it was constructed based on statistics was unfounded because grounds had not been put forward. That was my argument yesterday. Today, my learned friend very correctly, very correctly said, well, if Mr. Karnavas wants additional time he should put forward grounds. Well, I agree with that. But then the Prosecution should really put forward grounds that are not only predicated upon statistical evidence. Your Honour, it has been said in this courtroom before, and there may well have been more than a scintilla of truth in it - I don't deviate from that possibility at all - that some parties sometimes cry you a river. They were the words used, cry you a river. Well, if that proclivity is present for the Defence on occasion, one should not close one's mind to the possibility that the Prosecution may also cry you a river on occasions talking about their huge difficulties and the lack of time. But that emotive argument about being owed time and the unfairness shouldn't be a distraction to the substance, to the merits of a case put forward by a party; and one must always go back to legal principle. Your Honours, you do have a ruling. You've made a ruling in the past about allocation of time. You have made a ruling about the Defence allocation of time. I don't see any prejudice or reluctance or argument against giving the Defence additional time in re-examination if they have that time of their own in advance. It is for the Defence to best decide how to present its case, and if they subtract time from a witness that's to come in the future, to add time to a matter that they think is that important, Your Honours, in my submission, should be very slow to intervene. Your Honours, those are my submissions on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I suppose just to be consistent with the information we provide the Chamber about time and just to illustrate the point, this morning the Prosecution made very abbreviated and very measured comments that were not -- in no fashion personal at all to counsel; and so far, until I just stood up again, the Prosecution's comments were three minutes, three minutes. The Defence total time taken was 23 minutes. So about -- about eight times as much as the Prosecution's time. The point is made yet again. I disagree, Your Honour, fundamentally with Mr. Stewart. He says it's not personal, but when Mr. Stewart stands up and says I don't know -- such things as I don't know what Mr. Scott is so afraid, that's personal. And then when Mr. Khan gets up and makes similar things about, we should have a thicker skin, nobody should -- we shouldn't be saying these things, and then turns around and says -- talks about the Prosecution, Mr. Scott crying a river, I submit to you this morning, Your Honours, that the people who have been personal this morning throughout have been the Defence, not the Prosecution, and then had the gall, and then had the gall to criticise the Prosecution, and every comment -- personal comment this morning has come from the Defence side. Now, coming back to -- coming back to the merits, and I want to address some of the broader comments made. If the Chamber at one point wants to set time aside for other arguments, we can do that. I'm not going to address Mr. Prlic's comments. But Your Honour, this is a tempest in a teapot. What I said and what should have been heard and none of this was really necessary is, I'll say it again: I understand redirect flows from cross-examination. I understand that. Of course it does. That's the whole purpose of it. And I said a few minutes -- I said 23 minutes ago, I said 23 minutes ago, before the Defence started talking, that if Mr. Karnavas does need some additional time flowing from my hour, 35 minutes, of course he will ask for it, and he may be entitled to it. I hope I -- I hope I make some points on cross-examination. I certainly hope I do. And if Mr. Karnavas needs a few more minutes, then he can ask for that. My only -- the only observation I made that apparently has led to all this is that to stand up and say because the Prosecution gets another hour, 35, I will need -- I need to basically have the same time again, an hour, for additional redirect is I think -- I'd say preposterous and I think probably it is preposterous. That's the only comment I made. I don't rule out the possibility that Mr. Karnavas may seek a few additional minutes to respond to the additional time given to the Prosecution, for which, again, I'm most grateful. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Office of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, we'll stop there. This is a game of ping-pong, of table tennis. We have fully understood the problem. If you want to add anything else to the situation, well, I'll summarise the problem. Mr. Prlic wants an IC number for the document. He asked for that yesterday in the afternoon. We'll deliberate about that. There are two requests for interlocutory leave for appeal by Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Khan given this matter. We would like to have these requests in writing because the Chamber will take a written decision on the matter, as it's an important problem, so we need these submissions in writing, these requests in writing. The Prosecution will have 3 hours and 52 minutes as we have decided. Mr. Karnavas has requested four hours. The Chamber will deliberate about this on Monday, and we'll see whether he has the need for four hours for additional questions. We'll see about that. We'll discuss this among ourselves. Now, Mr. Stewart, I don't want to prevent you from speaking. Perhaps there was something else you wanted to address. If that is the case, I'll give you the floor, but if you just want to go over what we have been saying, it won't be necessary. It's for you to judge what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what I was going to say was intended to help to calm down the situation, but Your Honour has done that, so I have nothing more to say. Thank you. Thank you for the opportunity. I -- I don't take it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. We have almost lost 45 minutes by now, and if I say "lost," I must say we have not much -- heard much today that we haven't heard many times even before, so I did not think this very fruitful. I have, I must say, some hesitation in -- in -- that the custom that seems to come up that every decision of the Chamber gives rise to long discussions. It's not really what the administration of law is about. I would just like to recall to Mr. Karnavas what he said yesterday, and you find this on page 43, lines 9 and 10. I quote: "I hope that I wasn't in any way suggesting that the Prosecution should not," and here a word is missing, I think it's "get additional time." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I did also -- to be fair to me, I did say that they need to put their case forward, and as I argued yesterday and today, they haven't provided sufficient grounds other than statistics. So that was -- it was in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Prosecutor, I greet you again, and I give you the floor, and let's proceed in such a way that the witness can leave at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom, and to Mr. Batinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: If we go to March 2001, Mr. Batinic, did you hold any positions within the HDZ at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day to everyone, first of all. In March 2001, I was the vice-president of the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And a man named Ante Jelavic, was he the president of the HDZ at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this line of questioning. It's a waste of time. Where is the relevance? How does it fit within the indictment? How does it go to challenge this gentleman's credibility as to what occurred back in 1992, 1993? I'm objecting on the grounds that later on when they run out of time, they'll be asking for additional time as they've done with Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the purpose of the question, but the Prosecutor certainly has other questions that will follow, so let's wait to see what she'll say. Please proceed, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I will not be asking for additional time with this -- with this witness, just so that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, were you banned from political activities by the OHR in 2001, and was Ante Jelavic as well?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. There was a decision from the High Representative of the 7th of March, 2001, according to which I was banned from engaging in politics. But with your leave, I would like to provide you with an explanation. May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: We'll get to that. I just have a few questions before we get to that decision itself. Is it true that you and Mr. Jelavic were banned much on the basis of the same alleged facts put forward by the OHR?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What are the alleged facts, Your Honour? How is the gentleman supposed to guess what she's talking about? Yesterday we were talking about the OSCE, which is a different organisation than OHR.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'm now talking about the OHR. It's a different decision. This is a state-level decision, and I can go directly to -- to the decision removing Ante Jelavic from his position that he had at the time. These are decisions made by the OHR, not by the OSCE, just to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Could you please look at the small binder, Mr. Batinic, that you have there, and look up P 10662, please. Do you have the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Now, we see that up in the right-hand corner, it says that the date is 7th of March, 2001, and it has the logo of the office of the High Representative, and the deadline -- excuse me, the headline is: "Decision removing Ante Jelavic from his position as the Croat member of the BiH Presidency." And he was the Croat member of the BiH Presidency at the time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: We go down to the decision. You see that a bit further down. It says the following: "The decision is to remove Ante Jelavic from his position as member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to bar him from holding any official elective or appointive public office and from running in elections and from office within political parties unless or until such time as I may, by further decision, expressly authorise him to hold or seek the same." Do you recognise this decision regarding Jelavic, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'd just like to read out a couple of portions from this, and I'll ask you some questions in relation to that, and I'll ask you to go to page 3 of the B/C/S version, please, and that's the top of page 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is it, Mr. Praljak? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Judge Antonetti, while this political examination is in course and this political trial is continuing, allow me to remain in that room of mine over there. I don't want to participate in this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Try and act in this political way in America instead of terminating this trial here, because we're taking away the right to elections here without any proceedings. This is not understandable in Europe, in America.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen to what I have to say, Mr. Praljak. Sit down. Madam Prosecutor is cross-examining the witness, Mr. Prlic's witness. As you are well aware, she has the right to test the witness's credibility, which is what she is doing. Her objective is to discredit the witness in -- in the courtroom. It's a well-known technique. She's doing this on the basis of certain documents that I didn't know of. Allegedly, this individual, the individual concerned, was barred from participating in elections, and now the High Representative also took a decision, so that's what was explained to us. The witness said he was going to tell us what his point of view is. So let's wait to see what the witness has to say in response to the Prosecution's questions. I want to know why the High Representative barred him from engaging in political activities. This is not totally inoffensive, so let's remain calm and wait to see how things develop. That's the game. That's our practice. In your country, in my country, we would proceed differently; that's for sure, but this is how we proceed here. I didn't invent the rules. I'm applying the rules. Madam, unless I'm mistaken with regard to what you want to show or to demonstrate, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. I appreciate the fact that you fully explained the situation to my client. You also explained why you are allowing this line of questioning, which appears to be irrelevant [Realtime transcript read in error, "relevant"] to me and to my client, in spite of the fact that the Prosecution is trying to address the issue of credibility for this witness or the lack of credibility, but my client Mr. Praljak made a suggestion. He asked you to make it possible for him not to listen to this part of the examination. He finds it tantamount to torture. So since you provided him with this explanation, perhaps it will be good to ask him whether he would still like to remain outside of the courtroom until this part has been completed. But I think it's his right to request to leave the courtroom. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you for that explanation, Your Honours. Your explanation is the reason for which I don't want to listen to this. In the world today, given all the international resolutions, one accepts that without sentence, without a trial, in a certain country one can bar the person a right to vote or to participate in elections. I can't understand that this is being discussed. I feel ashamed because there's a military and incomprehensible administration there. The rights of this world, of this Tribunal, of France, et cetera, is being violated there because it says, for example, you without any laws, you don't have any rights. You don't have the rights of the citizen to be elected if you haven't been sentenced, if you don't have a criminal record. It goes back to the French Revolution. I understand that the Prosecution wants to ask this, but having fought for certain rights for many years and the right to such a trial, well, in that light I don't want to participate in this while this lasts, so please let me leave the courtroom. Because contrary to the Prosecution who wants to discredit the witness, I'm supporting the idea that the witness had certain rights, that the witness is a good man. Political opinions are being sanctioned in a Hitler-like decision. Please let me leave, not to listen to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you want to leave the courtroom, do so. I thought it would be better for you to stay here to listen to the witness's answer, but if you want to leave the courtroom for a while, go ahead. I'm not against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, here is the problem with what you're allowing the Prosecutor to do in this case. It's not a matter of trying to discredit the gentleman's credibility. You're now opening up an entire new issue, which perhaps most of you, if not all of you, are unaware you're doing. Now we're going into the politics in BiH post-Dayton and the aspirations of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina to be treated as an equal nation, which they feel they have been disenfranchised as a result of being put together in this federation where effectively they no longer choose their own leaders. This entire issue with Jelavic has to do with the Croats feeling that if Bosnia-Herzegovina is to survive, they should have a third entity. So there could be a Republika Srpska. There could be an entity for the Bosniaks and an entity for the Croats, and that's why the underlying issue behind Mr. Jelavic is this. And so now, it seems that we're into -- we're engaging into an area which has nothing to do with the trial itself, and I would -- that's why I ask, where are the parameters? At what point do we stop and say 1994, 1995. Now we're into 2001. How does this gentleman's rights affect his credibility? He wishes the place where he was born to be termed "Uskoplje" because that was the Croat name used before the Turks came into the area during the Ottoman Empire, and he's willing to have it called Gornji Vakuf/Uskoplje. For a variety of reasons, OSCE sanctioned him. Jelavic was elected, elected democratically. And when the nations that are running Bosnia didn't like it - that is, the OHR - they disenfranchise him. For what? Exercising his right to speak and his right to promote what he believed are the aspirations of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are political issues. These have nothing to do with this trial. We're here to see whether the Prosecution can prove its case, and that's why I'm suggesting that before we go into this area, we need to figure out, where are the parameters? Because then you're forcing us to put on a defence on issues that deal with politics, that deal with post-Dayton implementation, that have nothing to do with this case, with this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution -- Madam Prosecutor, a minute ago it was clear. I asked you whether the cross-examination had to do with the credibility of the witness. It seems that you said yes. Mr. Karnavas got on his feet and said it's a political matter. Madam Prosecutor, is this a matter of politics, or are you testing the witness's credibility? Mr. Scott can perhaps answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, and I apologise to my colleague who is obviously extremely capable, but because of the long history of these issues in this case and because of some of the comments that have been made my lead counsel on the other side, I think it's appropriate for me to address the matter, with the Court's indulgence. Thank you. Your Honour, this is not a new issue, and the fact that Mr. Karnavas hopefully, whether he intended to or not, perhaps has assisted the Chamber in seeing, in fact, the direct relevance of this issue. What this shows and what Mr. Karnavas has just, indeed, explained to the Chamber is the utter consistency of this political view and political Chamber, or political - excuse me - programme, political programme from 1991 to at least 2001 to create a Croat entity. We go back to the Livno question -- excuse me. We go back to the Livno question that we've seen again in the last few days, February 1992. "The formulation of the referendum we want is one of each constituent people in three separate areas (cantons)." It's exactly the same, and the only thing the Prosecution has said in response to Defence allegations along the way that this isn't, you know, this is not -- this is not relevant. This was only a temporary thing. It was only during the war. We never intended to do this. It's all been a long-term consistent programme, a third entity. A third entity. And that's the point. And this -- and as -- so that's one reason it's relevant. The second reason it's relevant is because it does go to the credibility of this witness. This -- the Chamber should know and -- you know, I'm not asking the Defence to agree with us. The measure is not whether anyone across the courtroom agrees with the Prosecution's case or not. I suspect they don't agree with the Prosecution case, but it does go -- we submit it does go to the credibility of this witness. This Chamber, the Judges, each of you should be able to -- should know in assessing the weight of this witness's evidence these matters. This is a witness who was highly Partisan, who has participated over time in the same Croat cause to create a third entity that goes back to November 1991: We want our sovereign Croatian territory, and the international community rejected that. Now, the Defence may not like that, but the people that the United Nations, the European Union, and the international community put in place to enforce Dayton said this is not permissible, and this man, the documents show, violated an act, committed and engaged in anti-Dayton activity. The Prosecution submits it goes to his credibility, and the Chamber should have the benefit of that information in assessing the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the third entity, first of all, has to do within the context of BiH. That's number one. Number two, how is it that the Serbs get to have Republika Srpska and the Croats cannot have their own entity? That's the issue now that we're getting into. This is a political issue. So let's take a country in Western Europe that may have three different speaking nations - let's say Italian, German, French - and we're going to disenfranchise one of them and say, No, two of you are going to be in one. That's -- now, effectively you had Mr. Tomic who said, Look, the federation wasn't being implemented the way it was envisaged. The Croats are still entitled to have political aspirations as a constituent nation. Having political aspirations is one thing. How did that go to his credibility as to what he was doing at the time that he testified about? Pose one question. Did OSCE or did OHR or did any other court issue any decisions against the gentleman for any activities that he carried out in 1991, 1992, 1993 when he was holding those positions for which he was testifying? That's the real issue, and what I'm afraid of -- and I'm perfectly capable of discussing these issues because I worked in Bosnia. They're very complicated, but we're turning this into a political trial. We're going away from what we're here for, and even if, even if in 2001 or 2006 - and I will show you a document later on about what is happening today in Bosnia-Herzegovina - even if the Croats today aspired to have a third entity within Bosnia-Herzegovina that guarantees their constituent rights as a constituent nation, it is not a crime; and that's why I think you have someone like General Praljak who feels offended by this sort of -- of a process because now we're politicising this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since we've raised the issue, I will speak quite calmly without any value judgements as to what was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina and why and who is to blame regarding the war, et cetera. The fact remains that one day in Dayton, under the leadership of the Americans, President Clinton and Holbrooke placed before the delegations a divided-up Bosnia-Herzegovina in which one people, the Serbs, were allotted 49 per cent of the territory after everything that had happened, and they were told, Here you are. This will be called Republika Srpska. Bosnia-Herzegovina is not even a republic. It's just called Bosnia and Herzegovina. Two peoples, the Croats and the Bosniaks, received 51 per cent of the territory with 43 per cent Bosniaks and 18 per cent Croats. So you add it up. So after everything that happened and, after all, you know quite a bit about it, the international community divided up Bosnia and Herzegovina in the ratio 49 to 51 per cent; and now all this suffering that we've seen from dozens of documents, the HZ HB sought only equality, and the thought that they might be entitled to certain cantons is being treated here as a crime. Isn't that absurd logically? If that is so, let's bring Holbrooke and Clinton, because they -- we were forced to make a federation in Bosnia-Herzegovina covering 51 per cent of the territory. This was after Srebrenica. It was after aggression, after Perisic, after everything that we have seen here for two years. Surely one's brain stops because it is so illogical. It is the logic of primary school. Bosnia and Herzegovina has been forcibly divided, statehood, the right to self-determination that was given to the Republika Srpska. You know what a republic is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, everyone knows what you are saying, so it's not a revelation. What I think is important is for you to wait and hear what the witness will say regarding the problem raised. I give you the floor, madam. Yes, Madam Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good morning to everyone, to Your Honours, and everyone in the courtroom. I feel it necessary on behalf of General Petkovic's Defence to say a few sentences for the simple reason that I think Scott has misrepresented the contents of certain documents, and I feel such misrepresentation at this point in time can have far-reaching consequences for the continued deliberations. Mr. Scott said that Dayton established that a third-Croat entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina was impermissible. Such a submission cannot be found in the Dayton documents or the discussions conducted there with which I am familiar. At the time, no discussion was conducted about the third entity because a year and a half earlier on after the Washington Agreement, the Croatian people agreed to enter into a federation with the Muslim federation. So this is a misrepresentation. I think it is not in dispute that the Albanian people of Kosovo had the right to separate from the state of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I interrupt you because I must state for the record that now we are hearing political speech after political speech, and this is an abuse of the publicity of this trial. These are all questions that can be discussed, and every opinion has pros and cons, but this is not the forum to do it, and I hope that the Prosecution will limit this line of questioning to the necessary. I think that a lot have been shown now. I think the Chamber has got an impression of what the political attitude of our witness is. As Mr. Karnavas has rightly pointed out, this is not something which is really directly going to his credibility. It shows his political views, but we think have abundantly heard what they are, and I would really wish that we could go on and terminate the questioning of this witness. I'm not silencing you, but I want this to be on record because I'm really feeling uneasy now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I fully understand your need to interrupt this debate, but your intervention was along the similar lines when you said that my colleague spoke along political lines. So I think your intervention is simply to stop a political debate. But Mr. Scott was not interrupted when he presented his political view that the Defence is saying that Herceg-Bosna was a temporary situation in the interest of the defence, and then he went on to say that its aim was a third entity, which was prohibited in Dayton, and this is a major crime for which the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina are to blame. I just wish to respond that a single political aim in itself cannot be a crime, and the attempt to organise a state as a federation, confederation, or anything else in itself cannot be a crime, but it is quite impermissible that Mr. Scott should be allowed to present certain political aims as a crime in itself. I would have plenty more to say on this issue, but I will sit down in the interest of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to correct the record. When I was speaking at the beginning of this discussion on page 24, line 18, the transcript says that this line of questioning is relevant in the opinion of myself and my client. That is not true. On the contrary. I said this line of questioning was irrelevant. But since I'm on my feet, let me add: On the basis of this discussion from the Prosecution on, you have finally seen for yourself that it is irrelevant. Let us stick to the rules, and let us do that. There are two possible reasons in theory and according to the law why the Prosecution may in the cross raise issues that relate to events far outside the scope of the indictment, much later than the indictment. It is either the question of credibility, and I think you've already ruled about that on the basis of Judge Trechsel's comments, or is it a -- or is it a continuation of something that happened in April 1993? But that is nonsensical. Then we have a sui generis form of mens rea, but we don't have actus reus anywhere in the indictment. So again, it's irrelevant. As for credibility, I'm not sure that it has been clearly stated that this witness is not mentioned in this document. He's not mentioned by name, nor does it refer to him; and we all know that as a result of these moves by the office of the High Commissioner, certain punitive measures were made and some people were acquitted, and in one case there is no ruling. So I repeat, there's no relevance to this line of questioning, and this is an example of a waste of court time. Your Honour, in view of the discussion, I feel that his last comment -- the last instruction he was given is not clearly translated. I don't think he was told that if he wishes to leave he may do so. Thank you. The document I'm referring is P 10662, P 10662.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber believes that the witness should respond. It's fine to listen to all of you, but what is important is the witness. Mr. Scott, you're going to reintervene to prolong the discussion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with great respect, that's exactly the problem. The Defence goes on and on. Everyone in the courtroom becomes impatient. The Judges become impatient, and I understand why, then when minutes and minutes later the Prosecution finally has a chance to be heard, then, Oh, it's -- the Prosecution's going to take more time. We've taken less time this morning than anybody else in the courtroom, substantially less. Now -- so yes, I do want to be heard. I do want to be treated fairly. I want the Prosecution to be treated fairly. Now, first of all -- first of all, I'm not expressing any political view. I've not expressed any political views this morning at all, and I'm not going to start now. Number one. Number two, a number of the Prosecution positions have been completely misstated, completely mischaracterised. I'm not going to go through them one by one, but I've heard counsel after counsel get on their feet and completely misstate the Prosecution's position and intentions and objectives. Number two. Number three, the Prosecution -- well, first let me go back. It does go to credibility, Your Honour, and to that -- to a very limited extent, I disagree a little bit with Judge Trechsel. It does go to credibility and bias. It goes to -- it goes to the Prosecution submits -- the Chamber will ultimately, of course, give the weight to every witness that they think is proper, and the Prosecution submits that in weighing -- in weighing the evidence of this witness, the Chamber should have this information, that this is a witness which we submit - the Chamber may disagree, but the Prosecution is entitled to put its case - we submit is a witness who is part and parcel, with great respect to the witness, of -- of this particular programme and -- and that we've seen, and the Prosecution -- the Chamber should be aware of that. It doesn't have to be a crime. It's a particular political view. It's a particular political bias. It doesn't have to be convicted of a crime to be relevant. It's information that the Chamber should have. Now, finally, Your Honours, finally, and -- and then -- and again, a response to Judge Trechsel's comment, and I take it fully on board. I'm not at all -- you know, sorry, Judge Trechsel. I'm not picking on you, but it's -- we never intended to belabour this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You may also pick. The others may pick on me. You have the same rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. I try not to, and I think the record -- well, the record will speak for itself. My only comment, Your Honour, is -- my only comment on that, Your Honour, the Prosecution never intended to belabour these points. My colleague has hardly had the opportunity this morning to put questions. We've put a few questions to the witness about a couple of documents. Had -- we would have been over by now. We would have been over by now if she would have simply been allowed to put a few questions. I've seen her outline. I've seen her outline. She only asked a few questions. She hasn't had a chance. Maybe belabouring it, but if we can please proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I wanted her to take the floor immediately. Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the document where we started out, Mr. Batinic. That's P 10662, the decision removing Ante Jelavic from his position on the BiH Presidency. And what I wanted to do was to read out the reason for the ban, and I'd like you to go to the B/C/S version, page 3, please, and it's the last paragraph, and it's the third last line, it should be, that starts with "Mr. Jelavic's unconstitutional behaviour." "Mr. Jelavic's unconstitutional behaviour culminated in his participation at what amounted to a party rally held at Mostar on 3rd of March, 2001, when those who participated were encouraged to make what was referred to as a 'decision' on the establishment on the" -- excuse me -- "the establishment of an unconstitutional and illegal parallel structure. Mr. Jelavic must have been fully aware that this 'gathering' under the name of a Croat national assembly was incapable of making legal decisions." Were you present at this gathering, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'd like to move to the decision that bans you from holding public and party offices, and that's actually -- it's a 1D document. It's number 1D 02800.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Maybe the usher can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Do you have it, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: This is a similar decision on the layout. We see up in the right-hand corner it's the same date, 7th of March, 2001, and it's again from the office of the High Representative, and it says: "Decision banning Zdravko Batinic from holding public and party offices." And I take it you recognise this decision, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And if we go down to the decision itself, there's a headline saying "Decision," it says: "To bar" -- "Decision to bar Mr. Zdravko Batinic from holding any official elective or appointive public office, and from running in elections, and from holding office within political parties, unless or until such time as I may, by further decision, expressly authorise him to hold or seek the same." And it says in the same paragraph that you also cease forthwith to be vice-president of the HDZ BiH. Those were the contents of this ban, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And if we go to the reasoning of the ban - that's continuing from where I was reading - it says: "Mr. Batinic has so conducted himself as to make it clear that he does not respect the institutions set up under the General Framework Agreement for Peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina and has thereby seriously obstructed the implementation of this Agreement. "On Friday, 2nd of March, 2001, the day before a 'gathering' in Mostar under the name of a 'Croat National Assembly' the High Representative issued a public appeal in which he clearly stated that any individual found to be engaged in illegal or anti-Dayton activities, including the establishment and maintenance of parallel structures, will be liable to sanction in accordance with my mandate." That should be the OHR mandate. "Activities aimed at undermining the legal institutions of the federation and state will not be tolerated." That gathering in Mostar, that's the same gathering as was referred to in the Jelavic decision, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a gathering. It was the Croatian National Assembly on the 3rd of March, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: But it's the same -- same -- the same incident or the same event that is referred to in the Jelavic decision, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Not just Mr. Jelavic. There were others too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And it goes on to say in the decision, and I'm reading from where I stopped before asking you the last question: "Mr. Batinic deliberately chose to ignore this warning and the repeated calls of the international community that all should work within the legal institutions of the country. The purported 'decisions' taken at Mostar on 3rd of March, 2001, are without legal effect but nevertheless represent a serious attempt to disrupt and undermine the constitutional order which prevails in the federation and in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Mr. Batinic has chosen to accept the position as so-called vice-president of the Croat self-government. By taking a leading position in support of such behaviour, Mr. Batinic must personally bear responsibility for his acts." It's correct, isn't it, that you did accept the position of vice-president of the Croat self-government as it says here?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the ban, this ban, was -- was lifted in whole in 2006 by the office of the High Representative as part of the closing-down process of that office?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office of the High Representative in Bosnia-Herzegovina has not been closed, and they decided to lift the ban on political activity of individuals who had been sanctioned. I assume they realised that they had been wrong all that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: That ban -- sorry, the lifting of the ban, that didn't only apply to you, did it? That applied to everyone that had been banned except for the persons who were banned for - let me call it - ICTY-related reasons?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the persons covered by the decision of the High Representative were relieved of this ban or the sanctions, and they were restored their basic human and civil rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And just one more short question before I assume the Trial Chamber would like to have a break, but the OHR did not only ban Croats, did it? They also banned Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OHR issued such bans to representatives of all three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina; but in relation to the total numbers of these peoples, the Croatian officials were the ones who had the most sanctions in relative terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: It would be a good time for the break, I believe, if that's in the Trial Chamber's mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We'll have a 20 -minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Based on something you said right before the break, Mr. Batinic, I'd like to show you one document, and that is number P 10663. That should be in the second binder. So in the -- in the smaller one. It's P 10663. That, Mr. Batinic, is, as you can see in the right-hand corner, again, from the 7th of July, 2006, and that's the decision lifting the ban from office within political parties in the removal decisions issued by the High Representative. And that should be the decision lifting the ban -- the whole of the ban that also applied to you. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And I'd like you to look at the decision itself, and it should be in the fourth paragraph of the decision. It says the following: "Noting that pursuant to the GFAP and the Conclusions, the High Representative has exercised his authority to remove officials from public office, thus far, on 160 occasions." Does that comply with your understanding that that number is correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the figure of 160 is correct, but I believe that the office of the High Representative knew the exact figures, and this is what they put down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Before the break, when I brought up this lifting of the ban with you, you said that -- and I'm quoting, "I assume they realised they'd been wrong all the time..." as I understood it referring to the OHR, then realising that they'd been wrong in applying the bans. I'd like to go to the next page of the document, please, the document you have in front of you. And in the English version, it's the second full paragraph on page 2 starting with "Profoundly convinced..." It should also come up on the screen in front of you, Mr. Batinic. And the OHR says as part of this decision to lift bans that it is: "Profoundly convinced that the broad prohibition contained in the Decisions removing public officials was necessary to meet the challenges confronting Bosnia and Herzegovina in its bid to restore peace, build institutions, consolidate national identity, bridge ethnic divides and work towards regional integration, all at an accelerated pace to overcome the retrograde momentum of the country's past." So here the office of the High Representative sets out that they thought it was necessary to imply these bans. Do you have any comment to that based on what you were saying before the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what is the relevance of all of this, what he may think about what the OHR was doing at the time? The gentleman did ask for an opportunity to explain why he did what he did and was not given the opportunity. Now he's being asked to comment about the office of the High Representative and their decisions. I don't see the point. Perhaps the question should be, Why were you banned? What were the crimes? What were the crimes for which you were banned? That's the real reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: If I -- if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He'll have the possibility of expressing himself. For the moment, I'm still waiting for his answer, but let the Prosecution proceed, and if the Prosecution doesn't put the question to the witness, I will. Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: The OHR says here that it thought it necessary to ban these people, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what they have noted here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: But your opinion is that that was wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, he should be given an opportunity to also read the part where they say: "... mindful, however, that the sanctions of a removal imposed against public officials pursuant to powers vested in the High Representative constitute an extraordinary measure interfering with certain rights of the persons concerned." We're talking about human rights. We're in Europe. This is modern day. So perhaps he should be given an opportunity to read that because that may go into his answer that he gave prior to the break. Let's be fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: With all due respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, your comment is only relevant to the extent that the witness was never familiar with the document. Witness, have you already seen this document before, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we received the decisions the High Representatives -- or High Representative individually when it came to decisions barring individuals from exercising political authority or participating in governmental bodies in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We never individually received a High Representative decision of this kind. I have heard about it, and many could download this decision from the website of the High Representative, but we didn't receive this decision individually. I just had a brief look at it, and the essence was that on the 31st of December, the ban was to be terminated. I didn't go into all the details, I have to admit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may add a small point, and I am a-addressing you, Mr. Karnavas. I also know a bit, something about the European human rights system. Interference is not at all the same as the violation. There are interferences all the time, so perhaps it doesn't quite have the weight that you seem to allocate to this word. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel, Mr. President. I wasn't planning to go into any other portions of this document. I'll leave it in the Trial Chamber's hands if the Judges have questions to the witness on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, I have a question. We saw this morning -- after a lot of meandering, we saw a decision from the High Representative, not the one that we have before us at the moment but a different one, banning all those who attended the Mostar meeting from being politically active; and here in 2006, there is a decision from another High Representative which revokes this decision. It refers to the prior decision, as well, but in fact the ban has been lifted here, and the decision states that there's reconciliation, the European Union, et cetera, et cetera, to be considered. You experienced all of this first-hand. You were concerned personally. So what reasons would you give for this change? First, you were banned from participating in politics; then the ban was lifted. What I would like to know is, in your opinion, what were the objections that were made against you exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I'd like to start from the beginning since yesterday in the afternoon the Prosecution tried to discredit my testimony when referring to the Decision of the Elective Council for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The decision of the council of the OSCE dated the 20th of July, 1998. The decision of The Electoral Council of the OSCE dated the 20th of July, 1998, in which I was banned from participating in the bodies of government in the Gornji Vakuf municipality. I was also banned from appearing as a candidate on the list of the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina just before the general elections in 1998, and I won't go on about that. This all had to do with the failure to implement the results of the elections in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf after the first local elections held after the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was in 1997. Why was I not prepared to implement the results of the election in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf? On the 29th of December, 1993, the Assembly of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna issued a law on amending the names of the municipality and town of Gornji Vakuf. It was to be changed to Uskoplje. On the 30th of March, 1994, at a session of the Constitutional Assembly of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a constitution for Bosnia and Herzegovina, for the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina was adopted in chapter 9 of the BiH federation constitution entitled "Transitional Solutions." In Article 5, paragraph 1, it states the following: All the laws and other regulations and judicial rules in force in the federation at the time that this constitution enters into force shall remain in force to the extent that they do not contradict the provisions of these constitutions, whereas -- and until the legal authorities do not decide otherwise. Before the first local elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1997, not a single joint body of government in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina revoked the law of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which referred to amending the name of the municipality and town of Gornji Vakuf, which was to be called the town and municipality of Uskoplje. All we did was request that the elections should be held for the municipality that was to be called Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, as a rule I understand things quickly, and I'll summarise the problem. Your municipality on the 29th of December, 1993, adopted an amended name. Gornji Vakuf was called Uskoplje. On the 30th of March, 1994, the federation at its meeting of the Constitutional Assembly stated as you have said in chapter 9, Article 5, paragraph 1, that everything that had been adopted previously would remain in force; and as a result, in constitutional terms, the change of name was confirmed, but this is not something that the High Representative liked, and he then decided to impose sanctions on you. But the High Representative, didn't he have the possibility of contesting the constitutional text that was adopted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the electoral commission took the -- the decision in 1998, not the Office of the High Representative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but this commission, didn't it have an appeals procedure or procedure that would have allowed them to control or supervise how legal this decision was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't aware of that possibility at the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With regard to the decision of the High Representative in Bosnia and Herzegovina on replacing Mr. Ante Jelavic, Zdravko Batinic, and three other colleagues of ours on the 7th of March, 2001, this is all related to the session of the Croatian national parliament in Mostar on the 3rd of March, 2001.
