With regard to this matter, I would like to state the following: Prior to the general elections held in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the year 2000, for reasons that were not clear to us Croats, the head of the organisation for Bosnia and Herzegovina, the organisation for European security and cooperation adopted a decision according to which the rules and regulations for elections of deputies were being changed, for the election of officials of that nation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina which had a two-chamber parliament, there's the House of Representatives and representatives are directly elected through elections, and there is the people's house or chamber which protests the vital interests of the people in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In his decision, the head of the European Organisation For Security and Cooperation terminated part of the constituent nation of the Croatian -- constituent nature of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The political leadership of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina responded by convening the Croatian national assembly in Novi Travnik in October 2000. At this Assembly in Novi Travnik, all important deputies were present. They had been elected at the previous elections, and these were deputies came -- that came from municipalities and from the state, the representatives from the Croats; there were representatives of the Catholic church and of cultural associations of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That session, a declaration was issued on the rights and on the positions of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Somewhat later, a decision was adopted according to with the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina should be called to participate in a referendum. The Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina had a referendum on the 11th of November, 2000. Over 90 per cent of the Croats who had come of age participated in the referendum and voted for the declaration on the rights and the positions of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. After the general elections that were held in November 2000, the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina won over 90 per cent of the Croatian votes in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In spite of that fact, the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina was not allowed to participate in the governmental bodies of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there is an article that states that municipalities and counties can link up in order to cooperate on an economic and cultural basis and for other reasons. The Croatian national assembly at its meeting of the 3rd of March, 2000, adopted a decision on associating municipalities and counties in which the inhabitants were mainly Croats or where the Croats were well represented. These decisions were supposed to enable some institutions of strategic importance for the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina to -- to survive, as they were to participate in financing these institutions. I have the Croatian university in Mostar in mind, the Croatian radio television of Herceg-Bosna and certain other institutions of particular importance for the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Croatian national assembly and the decisions that it passed in Mostar on the 3rd of March was the expression of the political opinion of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in that expression of the political opinion of the Croats, one wanted to warn everyone who dealt with Bosnia and Herzegovina that the basic rights of a constitutional people in Bosnia and Herzegovina were under threat and someone would have to deal with the issue. However, the international community through its then High Representative, Mr. Petritsch, acted as it did. They even selected us in a certain way and said that we were trying to overturn the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. McNair, a Canadian prosecutor, we were taken to trial at the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Chamber was composed of two international Judges and one Muslim Judge. This was supposed to be in our favour. After a certain period of time when they failed to provide evidence for the prosecution, the prosecution itself withdrew in March 2005. They gave up or, rather, the Judges, the trial decided to put an end to the trial against Ante Jelavic, Zdravko Batinic, Ivo Andric, Zuzanskic [phoen], Marko Topic, and Petar Milic. That would be all I have to say about this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Just one clarification on what you were just saying, Mr. Batinic. You referred to a trial, but that's different from the ban by the OHR, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is closely linked, Madam Prosecutor, as the decision of the High Representative says that it was anti-constitutional activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: But it was not the High Representative that brought a trial against you or, in fact, no trial was brought against you in the end, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to tell you in different terms. We were accused on the basis of the fact that the High Representative removed us on the basis of anti-constitutional activity, and we were put on trial; but as they were unable to prove anything, they withdrew the indictment themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The prosecutor, was he an international prosecutor or a national? And the Judges, were they nationals or internationals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at that point in time an indictment was issued against us by the international prosecutor, Mr. McNair, attached to the Prosecution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The trial chamber consisted of three Judges. Two were foreigners or, rather, they were not citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and one as I said to console us, a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina but a Muslim, a lady.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Moe. We can't see each other. A related question. What was the charge? Of what crime were you indicted, accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer, Your Honour, this question of yours. It wasn't clear to us, either, what we were charged with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Sometimes that happens, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. I'll move on to what is planned to be my last document that I'd like to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And that is, Mr. Batinic, number P 10621. It's a newspaper article. Do you have it, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And that is a newspaper article from Oslobodjenje from the 1st of March, 2001. So that would be right before these decisions by the OHR, time-wise, and it says: "Gathering in protest against Kordic and Cerkez judgement..." And it's a gathering that's supposed to have taken place in Busovaca. Were you present at this gathering?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present at this gathering.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Have you seen this particular article before?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't read Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Okay. I will read out -- this is about the gathering, the rally, and I'll read out some portions, and I'd like to ask you some questions in relation to that. It starts with saying that it's from Busovaca, and it says: "The president of the Croatian Democratic Union and member of the BH Presidency, Ante Jelavic, said that from Wednesday, the BH Federation would become a 'Bosniak entity' and called on Croats in BH to go to Mostar on Saturday to celebrate the session of the Croatian National Assembly, at which historic decisions would be adopted." Do you recall, Mr. Jelavic making that comment or something similar?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely what our president, Jelavic, said. We were there next to one another. I paid more attention to what others were saying, as I was familiar with the views of President Jelavic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: But this reference to go to Mostar on Saturday and reference to the session of the Croatian National Assembly, that's the same - I'll call it an event to try and be neutral - that was taking place on the 3rd of March, 2001, that we've seen references to in other documents, as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 3rd of March, the Croatian National Assembly met in Mostar, and it's not illogical that the president should call on those present to attend the rally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'd like to read out a different excerpt, and that should be in your B/C/S version, should be the third column and the second paragraph, I believe. In the English version, it is on page 2, and it's the first full paragraph, and it says the following: "Jelavic called on the Croatian people to come to the HNS, Croatian People's Party, Assembly on Saturday to celebrate the session in the name of Kordic, Blaskic, Cerkez, and all the other Croatian prisoners at which historic decisions will be adopted that will mark a new phase in Croatian freedom and equality." I'll first ask you if you remember Mr. Jelavic making that or a similar -- a comment to that -- a similar comment at the rally.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I don't remember the exact words used by Mr. Jelavic or anyone else who spoke at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: When I asked you about Mr. Jelavic's previous comment, the one I read out, you said that you were familiar with those views of his. Were you familiar with these views of his as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I'm going to ask for the relevancy. I don't believe this line of questioning was allowed or was conducted when -- for the Kosovo case, for instance, the Haradinaj, who was also allowed while on provisional release to politic, none of this while they were holding mass rallies for him -- proclaiming him to be a hero as the others that were being tried. What is the relevance of this, years later with the testimony that he has given about the time that is relevant to the indictment? I really fail to see the purpose of this. I'd like a ruling at this point in time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll be moving on. My general view is that this goes to the credibility of the witness, and I'll get to him in particular as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: A little bit further down, Mr. Batinic, it says, and that's about -- well, a little bit further. It's about two paragraphs further. It says: "In the main square in Busovaca where several thousand protesters had gathered, Ante Jelavic put forward the proposal to declare the Croats detained at The Hague heroes and men of greatness." Was that your opinion, as well, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again -- again, Your Honour, I'm going to object to this line of questioning. What does Jelavic have to do, what he thinks? What is -- I mean, I'd like a ruling, Your Honours. I made an objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor has just asked the witness what he thinks, whether he agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But what does it have to do with -- why is this relevant to the trial?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why is this relevant to the trial? That's the whole point. I'm objecting because I want a ruling. It is not relevant what Jelavic thinks, and since when is a public gathering impermissible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, there's a press article dated March 2001 which we have just discovered. There's a meeting following the judgement in the Kordic and Cerkez case. The witness is present. Jelavic is present. The journalist is telling us things. Maybe he's wrong. Maybe he's adding things. But as the witness was present, the Prosecutor is asking whether this is right. The witness says, "I don't know. I don't remember exactly what Mr. Jelavic said." Then the Prosecutor continues and asks him what his opinion is about this. Perhaps he has a point of view. Perhaps he hasn't. What is your intervention for? It is he who is testifying, not you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My intervention, Your Honour, is because we need to take control over this trial as to what is it that we're trying? Are we trying Mr. Jelavic for his political views?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the Judges who are ensuring control and not you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, then why are we discussing Mr. Jelavic's political views held at a rally in 2001? If you could point out to me where in the indictment Mr. Jelavic is and how his views in 2001 regarding a -- a decision made by this Tribunal, how that fits in. Many people are disappointed about the judgements that come out. So what? They're entitled to express their positions. But what does that have to do with this gentleman's credibility as to what he saw, what he heard, what he did in 1991, 1992, 1993? That's the relevant period of his testimony. That's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Prosecutor -- your objection has been recorded in the transcript. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Batinic, was based on the quote that I read out to you that Jelavic had put forward the proposal to declare the Croats detained at The Hague heroes and men of greatness, and then I asked you whether that was your opinion as well.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never had a serious discussion about that matter. I'm not sure that Mr. Jelavic said this, and if he did - which, I repeat, I'm not sure he did - it was because of the atmosphere at such a meeting. And generally, let me tell you, rallies of large numbers of supporters of a particular policy, all kinds of things can be said. What is important is the official policy, which is established at bodies and written down in documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. There is -- there is a quote from you in this article, or it's a reference to what you said, and that is if you go to page 2 of the article, page 2, so that would be the next page from what you're looking at right now, and it's the last paragraph in the first column. Do you see your name there? Last paragraph in the last column. Can you -- did you give an interview to Oslobodjenje, or did you take the floor, so to speak, and make a speech at this rally in Busovaca? And I'll read it out to you. I'm just asking you first if you can remember being interviewed or making a speech at this rally.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give an interview in those days that the beginning of March 2001 to Oslobodjenje. I did speak at the rally in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'd like to read out what it says here that you said, and I'll ask you a question after that. And it says: "Zdravko Batinic, vice-president of the BH HDZ, told the leaders of the world that the Croats could not be broken during the war, let alone in peacetime, and that Kordic's and Cerkez's sentences once more confirmed doubts about The Hague Tribunal, that not a single act had been proved and that they had tried the policies and the people. " And then there's a quotation mark starting, and this refers to you: '"These sentences have been handed down to all of us. We reject the qualifications presented in court about the HDZ being a nationalistic party, about the HVO being an aggressor force. This is a heinous frame-up by some people in the international community. We are proud to have participated in gaining Croatian freedom,' Batinic said. "He said that Croats must put up fierce resistance to these international leaders through wisdom and Croatian unity." Is that -- that's what you said at the rally, wasn't it, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke at the rally in Busovaca. I didn't send any message to any international leaders. I was addressing those present, and it is true that I said - and that is what I still think - that we are not a nationalist party, that is the HDZ of BiH. We are a peoples, a national party of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Croatian council was not an aggressor against Bosnia-Herzegovina, because I as a member of the armed forces of the HVO cannot be an aggressor in the country in which I was born, in which I live, and in which I work. It is my country.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Am I understanding you correctly, then, that these statements repeated in Oslobodjenje attributed to you, that's what you said at the rally?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that they took down precisely what I was saying, because bear in mind that the journalists of Oslobodjenje are mostly Bosniaks and that they mostly write things that correspond to their political views regarding the positions of the Croatian leaders. But the essence is what I have just said, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Just one more excerpt then, Mr. Batinic, that I'd like to show you. Can you recall Mr. Praljak being present at this rally?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that General Praljak was present. He may have been, but I don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'll read out one more portion to you of the article and see if that refreshes your memory, and that's the third column on the same page, and you can see there's a headline: "Including Stipe Mesic," and it says: "In his usual way, retired HV General Slobodan Praljak first held a brief history lesson about the last war and said that 'Alija Izetbegovic broke through to Central Bosnia after the Bosniaks had been slaughtered like cattle in Srebrenica.' "He added that Robert Barry was not the Croats' ruler, that Mate Granic cannot set up cantons in BH as he has done, and that the Croats do not recognise Stjepan Mesic." Do you recall Mr. Praljak making that statement at the rally?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I said a moment ago, I don't remember that General Praljak was present there. Then how can I remember his words?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I will leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And that concludes my cross-examination. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may [overlapping speakers] my redirect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. I have a follow-up question. Witness, the phrase that General Praljak may have said, I don't understand what it means. In the, text in the B/C/S, could you read it again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour. "Retired General of the Croatian army Slobodan Praljak, in his usual way, in addition to a brief history lesson regarding the last war, said that Alija Izetbegovic had reached Central Bosnia when the Bosniaks had been slaughtered like cattle in Srebrenica. "He added that the Croats' ruler is not Robert Barry, that Mate Granic cannot make cantons in Bosnia and Herzegovina as he has done, and that the Croats do not recognise Stjepan Mesic." End of quotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I will just pick up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that we would get this far, but we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, hope springs eternal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a lot of fear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just to help translate this part or at least clarify what General Praljak is saying with respect to Srebrenica, that was what had occurred with the Serbs and what happened to the Muslims in Srebrenica at the time or that actually began in 1992. There was an incident in 1992, 1993. There were -- that drove Muslims out of Srebrenica, that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct, Mr. Karnavas. In 1992 and 1993, the Muslims were in Srebrenica. They were slaughtered in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. In 1995 they were slaughtered, but when they moved towards Central Bosnia, the Serbs did drive Muslims to Central Bosnia as refugees, did they not, as they were setting up the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Karnavas. Most of the Bosniaks or Muslims, as they were known at the time, were expelled from Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Robert Barry was the head of OSCE at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Granic was associated with setting up the federation, which had envisaged cantons, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it says here, the Croats do not recognise Stipe Mesic. Mesic is from the Republic of Croatia, so I believe what Praljak is attempting to say is that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina do not recognise Stjepan Mesic, who is from another country, after all?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We didn't vote for Mesic. Therefore, he is not our president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "our president," meaning those of us in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the majority of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the enormous majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back a little bit because your credibility has been challenged, in other words, that you were lying about 1991, 1992, 1993, what you did, what you saw, what you experienced as a result of political thoughts or activities post-Dayton. So first, let me ask you this question. I'll go through them very quickly. The OSCE decision that we saw yesterday, were you given a hearing? Did you appear before this commission to actually give testimony, and were witnesses there to testify against you or on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never did anyone talk to me, not any one of those who finally made the decision to remove me from the bodies of authority of Gornji Vakuf, and especially not when they made the decision to bar me from being a candidate on the HDZ list prior to the general elections, and finally, something the Prosecution didn't mention but I will, all these documents, Your Honour, I gave to the Defence counsel so that everyone can use them. I have nothing to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And they would have been translated for the Trial Chamber's convenience, as well, some of them. Now, as far as -- as far as the OHR, did OHR provide you with a process, some due process, a hearing of some sorts prior to disenfranchising you, in a sense, taking your right away to engage in politics?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never did anyone call me, hear me, or discuss the matter with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- and before we go to the judgements that -- or the withdrawal of the charges that you spoke of, for the period that you testified about, that is, the period that's about this indictment, 1991, 1992, 1993, were you charged at all, either by OSCE, Barry and company - in this case it would have been Judge Finn Lynghjem who was running the subcommission for elections on behalf of OSCE - or OHR, were you ever charged for any illegal activity that you carried out in 1991, 1992, 1993, especially when you were acting as president of the Executive Council and as a member of the Crisis Staff and Presidency up there in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. None of the people you mentioned or any other bodies did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of a -- the withdrawal of the charges. If we could focus your attention to 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Usher, I will need your attention -- your assistance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could -- if you could look at 1D 02782. It's -- should be the third -- the third document in the binder. And -- do you have it, sir? 1D 02782. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And over here it talks about, this is a document which says it requests to withdraw the charges from the indictment. And if we look at the first paragraph, do you see your name there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And of course, we see the date of this is 8 March 2005. Was this the document that you were indicate -- you were talking about earlier, about the withdrawal of the charges from the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at the following document, which is 1D 02783. 1D 02783. Here, we have a ruling, and it's by a Steven Swanson. Under the statement of reasons, we see the indictment number KT-291/04.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we go to the previous document, Your Honours, you'll see that right above the name of Mr. Ante Jelavic. You'll see the same. It's a bit hard to find, to locate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was based on this ruling that the charges were completely withdrawn against you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, irrespective of your political views and position concerning the internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina held in 2000 -- in 1997, 1998, 2001 or even today, does that in any way, shape, or form change the substance of your answers to the questions that were posed to you on direct examination or from the Bench or from the Prosecution concerning the events of 1991, 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. I came to testify here at your invitation. I came to testify truthfully and to inform you of what I knew and of the events I had participated in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And your political views, the views that you hold today, for instance, or as of 2001, do they in any way change the substance of what is contained in the documents that were contemporaneously made back in 1991, 1992 that we saw and which you were participating in? The documents I'm referring to are those that were generated by the Presidency, the Crisis Staff, the Executive Council. Do your political views alter in any way the substance of what was contained in those documents?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They don't alter the substance in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, going back to the OSCE, the first document that we saw yesterday when they went after your credibility, we saw a gentleman -- another gentleman's name, Abdulah Topkic, I believe. Topcic.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who is this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Abdulah Topcic was the president of the SDA party as of the first multi-party elections held in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as of 1990, in fact; and he was also the president of the SDA in 1998. That's a year in which reference was made to the electoral commission of the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, during that -- those events back then in 1997, were you and Mr. Topcic somehow were trying -- were you trying to undermine the democratic process in any way in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I'm concerned, I wasn't trying to do that. I just insisted on using the name of the municipality, of using the name Uskoplje, too, because historically speaking, that was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday there was some questions asked of you about the Croats aspiring, I underscore that, aspiring to be a constituent nation. That's how it appeared from the Prosecution, and you told us that there was no need to aspire, that the Croats were in fact a constituent nation as were the Serbs and the Muslims, now Bosniaks, in Bosnia and Herzegovina; and in fact, you said every square inch or foot or metre in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So -- and then you were asked some questions about the -- the -- what was envisaged by the HDZ platform. So now I want to show you a document, 1D 00398. This is the -- goes to the Cutileiro Plan. And we don't have the -- I'm told that we don't have the B/C/S, so I will read that part for you and see -- and then ask you to comment on it. My apologies for not having it -- having it in your language. It says at the beginning, it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm reading from page 24, Your Honours. You'll find that on the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It says: "In Bosnia" -- "Bosnia and Herzegovina would be a state composed of three constituent units based on national principles and taking into account economic, geographic, and other criteria." It then goes on to say that the existing border would continue. And then it says: "Sovereignty resides in the citizens of the Muslim, Serb, and Croat nations and other nations and nationalities who realise it through their civic participation in the constituent units and the central organs of the republic." And let me read one other part before I ask you the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On page 26, Your Honours, a couple of pages further down where -- where the title D. The constituent units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "1. Within Bosnia and Herzegovina, constituent units would be established, which are defined in part E below." If we go to part E, it reads: "A working group will be established in order to define the territory of the constituent units based on national principles and taking into account economic, geographic, and other criteria." Now, could you please tell us, how different is what is proposed by Cutileiro at this time, one of the international players, and what was being -- what was part of the platform for HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our opinion, there was no difference. This Cutileiro Plan or proposal for the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina followed our political thoughts and proposals that we put forward when it comes to the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me go on to the next document, 1D 00526. This deals with the Stoltenberg -- it should be the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. And again, I must apologise. I don't have the Croatian version, but I will read the relevant parts. They're very short, and hopefully you'll be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could -- if I could draw your attention at the very -- at the top of the page. It's 286, 286 of this particular document, and you'll see under Roman numeral I, it talks about -- it says "Constitutional agreement of the union of republics, Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it says, I'll just read the first part: "The constitutional agreement of the union of republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina is set out in appendix I hereto." And then it goes on about this agreement. Now, if you go further down and -- and we go to appendix I, and that would be on 290. It started off with Article 1 under "The union of republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina..." we see it says: "The union of republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina is composed of three constituent republics and encompass three constituent peoples..." I underscore "constituent" so we don't have to, hopefully, deal with this issue again. "... and the constituent peoples are, according to Article 1 by Owen-Stoltenberg, the Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, as well as groups of others. The union of republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be a member of the state of the United Nations..." And it goes on. And then if we turn to Article 2 under Roman numeral II, which is the constituent republics and their responsibilities, it says: "Each of the constituent republics shall adopt its own constitution which shall provide for democratic forms of government including democratically elected legislatures..." and so on. And then if we look at Article 3, it says: "All government functions and powers, except those," "except those assigned by the constitutional agreement to the union of republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina or to any of its institutions shall be those of the constituent republics."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honours, if you go to page 29 -- 294 and on to 295, we see under Roman numeral V, "Human rights and fundamental principles."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And -- and so my question now to you, sir, is having just read parts of this agreement that was being proposed by the internationals, which recognised that there are three constituent peoples, nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, how different is that from the platform which was being advanced by the HDZ at that time? How different is it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a Croatian version of the Cutileiro -- or, rather, Vance-Owen Plan, but in the light of what you have just said, there is absolutely no difference between the platform of the BH HDZ and this plan for the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I was reading, actually, from the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. The Vance-Owen is slightly different, but --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- [overlapping speakers] basically what we're talking about -- essentially what was in the platform is in these proposals by the internationals themselves, right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like to emphasise a very important fact. In each peace plan, it was explicitly stated that it was a peace plan for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there was an attempt to find a solution for its internal organisation, and it was explicitly stated that the constituent peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina were the Croats, Serbs, and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One final question. There won't be any need to go to any of the other documents. Just one final question. Sir, at the time that you were serving in the Executive Council for Gornji Vakuf, did you do anything to undermine the lawful authorities of Gornji Vakuf of which you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. I did my utmost. I acted to the best of my ability and strove to ensure that things ran smoothly in the area of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf, that they ran normally. We wanted to have good cooperation between the two ethnic groups, and we didn't want any incidents to break out. I really did my utmost.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And have you testified truthfully here today, yesterday, and the day before, and the day before that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a solemn declaration, and I have spoken the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to thank you, Mr. Batinic, for coming here to give your evidence. Good luck, and have a safe trip back home.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask my colleagues whether they have any questions, follow-up questions. Very well. Mr. Batinic, I would like to thank you on behalf of my colleagues to have come to testify here and to answer all of the various questions put to you by Mr. Karnavas, by the Defence, by the Prosecution, by the Judges. I wish you a safe trip home, and I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, and I would like to greet everyone here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As everyone knows, according to the schedule for next week, we'll have Mr. Neven Tomic on the 17th and 18th. We should conclude with him on the 18th, and we should hope that there won't be any objections or various problems that will require additional time. Mr. Tomic is very busy. He's already been here once. He's coming here for the second time now, and I think that Monday and Tuesday should be sufficient for us to conclude with the hearing of this witness. The week afterwards, after that week, well, there shouldn't really be any problems that week. Mr. Scott, are there any other matters you would like to address apart from the matters addressed this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There was just a few more points I really wanted to make, Your Honour. No, Your Honour, I think we're done for the week. I think everyone wants to be done for the week. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Judge Antonetti, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was saying that I hope everyone will have a good rest for next week. We will commence our hearing on Monday at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of November, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.11 p.m.,
